# Emergence of a Distinct Mechanism of C–N Bond Formation in Photoenzymes

**Authors:** Felix C. Raps; Ariadna Rivas-Souchet; Chey M. Jones; Todd K. Hyster

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, 08544 United States. | 2 Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, 14853 United States. | 3 Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, 07065, New Jersey, United States.

## Abstract

C–N bond formation is integral to modern chemical synthesis due to the ubiquity of nitrogen heterocycles in small-molecule pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Alkene hydroamination with unactivated alkenes is an atom economical strategy for constructing these bonds. However, these reactions are challenging to render asymmetric when preparing fully substituted carbon stereocenters. Here, we report a photoenzymatic alkene hydroamination to prepare 2,2-disubstituted pyrrolidines by a Baeyer-Villiger Monooxygenase. Five rounds of protein engineering afforded a mutant, providing excellent product yield and stereoselectivity. Unlike related photochemical hydroaminations, which rely on the oxidation of the amine or alkene for C–N bond formation, this work exploits a through-space interaction of a reductively generated benzylic radical and the nitrogen lone pair. This antibonding interaction lowers the oxidation potential of the radical, enabling electron transfer to the flavin cofactor. Experiments indicate that the enzyme microenvironment is essential in enabling a novel C–N bond formation mechanism with no parallel in small molecule catalysis. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate the substrate in the enzyme active site which further support this hypothesis. This work is a rare example of an emerging mechanism in non-natural biocatalysis, where an enzyme has access to a mechanism that its individual components do not. Our study showcases the potential of enhancing emergent mechanisms using protein engineering to provide unique mechanistic solutions to unanswered challenges in chemical synthesis.

Enzymes are ideal scaffolds for chemical synthesis because they use an ensemble of covalent and non-covalent interactions between reactive intermediates and the protein to facilitate transformations.1 These contacts enable enzymes to carry out transformations with unparalleled levels of selectivity and perform reaction mechanisms that are inaccessible to cofactors or minimalist proteins.2 A complex system with access to mechanisms whose individual parts do not display a property is known as emergence.3 The phenomenon of emerging mechanisms is well known for native enzyme function but is rare when using enzymes for non-natural reactivity.4–7 Examples include P411-catalyzed nitrene insertion into C–H bonds and bicyclobutane formation,8 higher-order charge transfer complexes with flavin-dependent oxidoreductases,9 and mesolytic cleavage of nitroradical anions in reductive couplings using ‘ene’-reductases.10 While emerging mechanisms are challenging to predict, when discovered and optimized using protein engineering, it has the potential to unlock new reactions and retrosynthetic disconnections.11

Hydroamination of alkenes with unactivated amines is an atom economical strategy for constructing new C–N bonds.12,13 These seemingly simple transformations are, however, challenging to implement when moving beyond model substrates. For example, the asymmetric construction of α-tertiary amines by coupling 1,1-disubstituted alkenes with amines via a Markovnikov hydroamination remains a significant challenge.14 Transition metals, the most common hydroamination catalysts, are poorly suited for constructing sterically hindered bonds.15,16 Reactions involving radical intermediates are functional group tolerant, but form exclusively the anti-Markovnikov product and are challenging to render asymmetric in the C–N bond-forming event (Figure 1a).17 Alternatively, Brønsted acid catalysts were recently reported to catalyze this transformation but suffer poor functional group tolerance and require deactivated amines with directing groups to achieve enantioselectivity.18 We envisioned enzymes to be ideally suited for this type of reaction, however, there are no known biocatalysts capable of catalyzing hydroaminations with unactivated amines and alkenes. Given their high reactivity, compatibility with aqueous conditions, and substrate tolerance, we envisioned radicals as ideal intermediates for the desired reaction. However, the enzyme will need to utilize a unique mechanism to override the inherent regioselectivity of known radical mechanisms of C–N bond formation.

We targeted the development of an enzyme-catalyzed intramolecular hydroamination to prepare 2,2-disubstituted pyrrolidines (Figure 1b). Our group and others have demonstrated that flavin-dependent ‘ene’-reductases can catalyze various C–C,10,19–22 N–C,23,24 and C–O25 bond-forming reactions with regio- and enantioselectivities that can be tuned using protein engineering. A common feature of these reactions is the need for activated radical precursors, such as alkyl halides and hydroxamic esters, which, upon reduction, undergo an irreversible bond cleavage to ensure that productive chemistry is competitive with back electron transfer. In this study, we targeted a photoenzymatic process involving unactivated radical precursors, a challenge that needs to be overcome to increase the synthetic utility of photoenzymatic processes.

We began by exploring the radical cyclization with the model substrate 1 based on its ability to form products via a 5-exo-trig or 6-endo-trig cyclization (Figure 2a). A library of flavoenzymes was compiled based on the hypothesis that an enzyme that naturally catalyzes an oxidative transformation would best tolerate the anticipated radicals generated in the active site.6,26 We found that monoamine oxidase (MAO-N-D11C)27, styrene monooxygenase (StyA1)28, D-amino acid oxidase (AcDAAO)29, choline oxidase (AcCO6)30, and cholesterol oxidase (ShCO)31 were unable to cyclize a hydroamination reaction when irradiated with blue light. In contrast, a cyclohexanone monooxygenase from Acinetobacter calcoaceticus (AcCHMO) showed low conversion to the 5-exo-trig hydroamination product 2 (1% yield, 55:45 e.r.) without forming the 6-endo-trig product 3, the product formed when using aminyl or aminium radical cations (Supplemental Figure S6).32 Control experiments confirmed that CHMO and light were necessary for reactivity and that free FAD could not facilitate this transformation. To improve this activity, we built a library of CHMO homologs and found that an omeprazole sulfoxidase reported by Zhao et al. (AcCHMO-M10) afforded product in 12% yield and 55:45 e.r.33–35

With initial activity in hand, we engaged in a protein engineering campaign using iterative site saturation mutagenesis (ISM) following a reduced codon strategy to increase the yield and enantioselectivity of the reaction.6,7,36 Sites for mutagenesis were selected based on their proximity to the cofactor. To aid in selecting the sites for mutagenesis, we used a structure predicted by AlphaFold 2.0 which was modeled onto a crystal structure of ancestor AcCHMO-M2 (pdb 6a37).35,37 We began by targeting residues within 4 Å of the flavin cofactor (Figure 2b–c). Mutation of arginine at position 327 to lysine (R327K) increased the yield to 22% with 71:29 e.r. Further rounds of mutagenesis identified sequential mutations R490E (45%, 70:30 e.r.), C326H (56%, 81:19 e.r.), and I491T (71%, 93:7 e.r.). These three positions are all situated in the substrate channel leading to the active site presumably tailoring the position of the substrate during the reaction. Finally, mutation of alanine at position 479 to histidine (A479H) led to product formation in high yield and excellent enantioselectivity (97%, 95:5 e.r.). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that the three distal mutations – R490E, I491T, A479H – reside in a dynamic loop region (residues 475–510) that gates access to the enzyme’s active site (Figure 2d). This loop resembles the “control loop” region that was investigated in homologous RmCHMO.38 In the parent enzyme, this flexible loop forms interactions (e.g., between R490 and Q210) that close the active site entrance. The introduction of these distal mutations appears to disrupt interactions between the active site-gating loop and other regions of the enzyme, which prevents the loop from shielding the active site. Thus, it is likely that the R490E, I491T and A479H mutations play an important role in keeping the active site open and accessible to substrates – a plausible explanation for the ~15–30% yield improvements associated with these mutations.

The efficacy of the enzyme to catalyze the reaction was tested in cell-free, dialyzed lysate by lowering the catalyst loading to 0.04 mol% (Figure 2a, entry 3). The reaction still proceeded in modest amounts (17%, TON= 436), forming the product 4 retaining the enantiomeric ratio. We observed in the undialyzed lysate (1 mol%) a diminished enantiomeric ratio (93:7) of the product. When considering possible inhibitors, we recognized NADP+ as a potential candidate based on its role in the natural mechanism.34 When 0.1 equivalents of NADP+ relative to enzyme was added to the reaction, the yield decreased to 63% with a decrease in enantioselectivity to 93:7 e.r. Addition of equimolar amounts of NADP+ to enzyme (1.0 equivalents of NADP+ relative to enzyme) entirely impedes the reaction, suggesting that NADP+ binding is inhibitory. This is distinct from the native reactivity, which requires both FADH and NADP+.34

The final enzyme —dubbed AcHYAM (HYdro AMinase)— was tested for its proficiency in catalyzing the cyclization on several substrates (Figure 3). Various aniline and styryl substitutions were tolerated, with electron-rich arenes generally affording higher yields and selectivity (2; 4–10, 13–20). Large substituents, such as naphthalenes, on the aniline side (10) and the styrene moiety (19) did not diminish the yield and were transformed with excellent enantioselectivities. Additionally, electron-deficient nitrogen-containing heterocycles are tolerated (11–12, 21), overcoming a limitation to Brønsted acid-catalyzed cyclization. The cyclization was sensitive to the heterocyclic substitution and severely hampered in some cases (Supplemental Figure S1). Nevertheless, protein engineering might allow to overcome these limitations. The homologated substrate can engage in a 6-exo-trig cyclization to afford product 22 in 13% yield with promising levels of enantioselectivity (78:22 e.r.). This particular example is fascinating because, when using a photoredox catalyst, this type of substrate could typically undergo a 1,5-HAT event over cyclization.40 Modifications to the backbone of the pyrrolidines were tolerated with the dimethyl substitution 23 obtained in moderate yield (42%) and enantiomeric ratio (27:73 e.r.).

Next, we used this method to prepare α-methylated analog of three aryl pyrrolidine-containing APIs. The methylated pyrrolidine fragment of TRK inhibitor GNF-862541 was obtained in excellent yield (24, 85%, 94:6 e.r.), as well as the fragments of modified Tropomyosin inhibitor α-methyl Larotrectinib (26, 77%, 75:25 e.r.),42 and related structure (25, 25%, 73:27 e.r.).43 These syntheses demonstrate the ease with which this method can prepare substituted analogs that typically involve multistep sequences.

Next, we investigated the mechanism of the reaction. At the onset, we hypothesized that an enzymatic hydroamination would initiate the reaction via substrate oxidation, however, the observation of an induction period suggested that oxidized flavin is not responsible for radical initiation and instead, needs to be photoreduced for the reaction to occur (Supplemental Figure S2). To determine whether a reduced oxidation state of flavin was responsible for radical initiation, we ran the model reaction with the enzyme pre-reduced by sodium dithionite and observed product formation in 74% yield with 95:5 er and loss of the induction period (Supplemental Figure S3).44 Importantly, the UV-Vis spectrum produced when the enzyme is reduced by dithionite is identical to the one observed when the enzyme is photoreduced by buffer, indicating that both conditions produce the same flavin oxidation state (Supplemental Figure S4 & Figure S5). These results reveal that the observed induction period was due to the requirement for photoreduction45 of FAD to FADhq, indicating that the reaction initiates from the reduced form of the cofactor. These results exclude a nitrogen-centered radical as the reactive intermediate, as only an oxidizing photocatalyst could form this species. Indeed, when aniline 1 is subjected to literature known reaction conditions for generating aminium radical cations, only the product of a 6-exo-trig cyclization is observed, inconsistent with the results from the enzymatic reaction (Supplemental Figure S6).46,

Next, we considered whether reduced flavin was serving as an energy transfer catalyst.47 Lewis et al. described a related 5-exo-trig hydroamination by direct excitation at 281 nm in the absence of a photocatalyst (Supplemental Figure S7).48 They invoked a diradical combination as being responsible for the bond-forming event and substantiated their hypothesis by observing fragmentation in a derivative substrate. To probe any diradical character in the enzymatic reaction, a related fragmentation substrate (Supplement substrate S40) was subjected to the enzymatic reaction conditions, and samples were analyzed using GC-MS and NMR. No evidence for fragmentation was observed, suggesting that an energy transfer mechanism is unlikely.

Based on the need for reduced flavin and the lack of evidence for an energy transfer mechanism, we concluded that alkene reduction by FADhq* (E0= −2.26 V v. SCE) is responsible for radical initiation (Figure 4a).21 While this potential should not be sufficient to reduce the substrate (α-methyl styrene Ered= −2.6 V v. SCE),49 the electropositive active site can attenuate the potential required to reduce the alkene while also stabilizing the resulting anionic flavin semiquinone (FADsq−) (Figure 4b).50 The resulting radical anion is highly basic, leading to a fast and irreversible protonation, resulting in benzylic radical formation. While we initially hypothesized that this radical is oxidized to the corresponding benzylic cation, substates bearing other nucleophilic species, such as a primary alcohol 27, an alkylamine 28, and a methyl-substituted alkene derivative 29 are completely unreactive (Figure 4c). This observation is inconsistent with a tertiary carbocation and suggests a π-π stacking interaction is required for the reaction to proceed. When considering other mechanistic possibilities for C–N bond formation, we hypothesized that an interaction between the aniline and benzylic radical could alter the redox properties of the system. While this type of transannular interaction is unknown in the literature, it is well known that hyperconjugative interactions between lone pairs and radicals will increase the energy of the singly occupied molecular orbital (SOMO), making the radical easier to oxidize.51 If the protein were to template this interaction and overcome the repulsive electronic forces by confining the substrate in a reactive conformer, a similar redox activation would be expected. We calculated the frontier molecular orbital configuration of the preorganized intermediate by density functional theory (DFT) (Figure 4d). The prealigned structure was determined by performing a coordinate scan of the product in its doublet state. The C–N bond was pulled apart in iterations to identify an energetic minimum, which was optimized at M06-D3(0)/6–311+G(d,p) level of theory.52 The resulting SOMO populates an antibonding configuration with the orbitals out of phase for a C–N bond formation with significant character on the styrenyl arene. However, the HOMO-1 has bonding character between the aniline nitrogen and benzylic radical with significant orbital coefficients on the aniline arene, supporting our hypothesis that this type of n → SOMO can lead to bonding character. The oxidation potentials of the preorganized and open chain structures were determined by DFT using the Born-Haber relation. The oxidation potential of the unaligned form was closely matching to the benzylic α-methyl styrenyl radical (Supplemental Figure S8). In the calculated, prealigned structure, the oxidation potential was found to be significantly lowered (ΔEox= −0.70 V v. SCE). This feature is vital because FADsq− is insufficiently oxidizing (E0= −0.25 V v. SCE)53 to produce a benzylic carbocation from the corresponding radical (Eox= 0.16 V v. SCE).51

Based on the observed reactivity and the gathered mechanistic evidence, we conclude that the enzyme facilitates this hydroamination using a mechanism that is distinct from small molecule catalysis. This emergent mechanism relies on the repulsive interactions from a formal two-center three-electron antibonding intermediate to attenuate the oxidation potential of the radical within the enzyme active site. We hypothesized that this interaction is only possible because of the preorganization provided by the protein. Surprisingly, MD simulations suggest that the AcHYAM environment provides the model substrate with more rotational freedom relative to the parent enzyme. However, we see evidence of substrate conformations in AcHYAM that resemble the preorganized conformation investigated by DFT (Figure 5a), which are sparsely observed in the parent enzyme. Mutations near the catalytic site (i.e., R327K, C326H) are likely responsible for this enhanced conformational flexibility, as the substrate predominantly samples extended conformations in the parent enzyme. We concluded that the new rotational freedom allows for the substrate in the engineered AcHYAM environment to orient itself into the conformation crucial for C–N bond formation.

Indeed, when a photoredox reaction was conducted with 10-phenylphenothiazine, a photocatalyst reported to reduce α-methyl styrene to the corresponding radical anion,55 no 5-exo-trig product was observed (Figure 5b). When the same reaction is conducted in the presence of a thiol catalyst, alkene reduction was found in 34% yield, indicating that despite the ability of 10-phenylphenothiazine to reduce the alkene of 1 to the radical anion, no C–N bond formation occurs without the templating provided.

In conclusion, we have developed a highly selective photoenzyme for a stereoselective hydroamination using anilines. Based on experiments and calculations, we conclude that this reaction utilizes a previously unknown mechanism for C–N bond formation, which is enabled by the preorganization provided by the protein active site. This emergent mechanism of C–N bond formation highlights the opportunity for enzymes to reveal new pathways which can be used to address reactivity challenges in chemical synthesis.

9 Abstract – Biocatalysis has revolutionized chemical synthesis, providing sustainable methods for

10 preparing various organic molecules. In enzyme-mediated organic synthesis, most reactions

11 involve molecules operating from their ground states. Over the past twenty-five years, there has

12 been an increased interest in enzymatic processes that utilize electronically excited states

13 accessed through photoexcitation. These photobiocatalytic processes involve a diverse array of

14 reaction mechanisms that are complementary to one another. This comprehensive review will

15 describe the state-of-the-art strategies in photobiocatalysis for organic synthesis until December

16 2022. Apart from reviewing the relevant literature, a central goal of this review is to delineate the

17 mechanistic differences between the general strategies employed in the field. We will organize

18 this review based on the relationship between the photochemical step and the enzymatic

19 transformations. The review will include mechanistic studies, substrate scope, and protein

20 optimization strategies. By clearly defining mechanistically distinct strategies in photobiocatalytic

21 chemistry, we hope to illuminate future synthetic opportunities in the area.

56 1.0 Introduction 57

58 Enzymes are attractive catalysts for chemical synthesis because they carry out

59 transformations with catalyst efficiencies and reaction selectivity that surpass what is possible

60 with small molecule catalysts.1 A traditional workflow involves identifying an enzyme that can

61 catalyze the desired reaction on your substrate of interest. If the starting enzyme fails to provide

62 the desired results (activity, enantioselectivity, solvent tolerance, etc.), directed evolution can

63 optimize the protein's function.2,3 The advent of sophisticated techniques for generating mutant

64 libraries and advances in analytic chemistry has accelerated protein engineering to the point

65 where biocatalysts are now considered competitive alternatives to traditional small molecular

66 catalysts for reactions such as asymmetric ketone reduction and reductive amination.4,5 Moreover,

67 enzymes are now commonly used in chemical manufacturing to streamline the synthesis of

68 pharmaceuticals.6,7,8,9

69 As biocatalysis develops as a tool for synthetic organic chemists, enzymes need to

70 catalyze new types of reactions.10,11 As the in-silico design of enzymes remains challenging,12,13

71 new biocatalytic reactions are typically developed by mining natural product pathways to

72 discover enzymes that catalyze new types of transformations. However, as nature is conservative

73 in its synthetic strategies, enzymes catalyze far fewer reactions than small molecule transition

74 metal catalysts or organocatalysts. Consequently, efforts have been focused on discovering

75 enzymes that possess unrealized catalytic potential.

76 Over the past fifteen years, visible light photocatalysis has reemerged as a powerful

77 platform in chemical synthesis.14,15 In these reactions, a photocatalyst, typically an organic dye or

78 transition metal complex, is photoexcited to access an electronically excited state which can

79 engage in electron or energy transfer events to form radical intermediates. This activation mode

80 has enabled countless synthetic reactions. Moreover, merging photocatalysis with transition

81 metal catalysis or organocatalysis allows for reactions that are inaccessible to either catalyst

82 individually.16,17 These reports have spurred interest in using light with enzymes. Nature uses light

83 in many different contexts. In photosynthesis, large multiprotein complexes convert photonic


<!-- Page 5 -->


84 energy to chemical energy to sustain life. Alternatively, light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) domains use

85 light to induce conformation changes to regulate proteins and enzymes. Interestingly, only three

86 enzymes are known in nature to absorb sunlight to promote a chemical reaction; DNA

87 photolyase,18 fatty acid photodecarboxylase,19 and protochlorophyllide reductase.20 While this

88 activation mode is rare, these enzymes showcase how enzymes use light to facilitate biologically

89 essential transformations.

90 The burgeoning area of “photobiocatalysis” is focused on developing new biocatalytic

91 reactions that involve light.21,22,23,24 This review will organize reports based on the relationship

92 between the photochemical step and enzymatic transformation. We will define key concepts and

93 focus on mechanistic nuances that make strategies distinct from one another. By clearly defining

94 the mechanistic differences between various approaches, we hope to contribute to the overall

95 understanding of how light can be used in biocatalytic synthesis.

96 The first section will focus on photoenzymatic catalysis. We define photoenzymatic

97 catalysis as reactions where a cofactor, located within the protein active site, is photoexcited to

98 promote electron or energy transfer required for the conversion of starting material to product

99 (Figure 1A). Discussion of this topic will be focused on enzymes of value for synthetic organic

100 chemistry. The second section will explore synergistic photoenzymatic catalysis (Figure 1B).

101 These reactions involve the excitation of an exogenous cofactor to enable a chemical

102 transformation within a protein active site. The third section will focus on photobiocatalytic

103 cascades (Figure 1C). In these reactions, the photochemical transformation occurs in the

104 presence of the enzyme but is not involved in the enzyme's mechanism for converting starting

105 material to product. This section will contain four subsections; i) reactions where light is used for

106 cofactor regeneration, ii) reactions where photoexcitation is involved in modifying the substrate

107 of the enzyme in a one-pot, one-step process, iii) reactions where photoexcitation modifies the

108 substrate in a one-pot, two-step process. In the final section, we will discuss whole-cell

109 photobiocatalytic reactions that use light with cyanobacteria to produce NADPH that enzymes

110 can consume to reduce substrates (Figure 1D). In clearly defining these terms, we hope to

116 2.0 Photoenzymatic Catalysis 117

118 Photoenzymatic processes are reactions where a cofactor or amino acid side chain within

119 an enzyme absorbs light and uses the photonic energy to convert starting material to product.25

120 While this general mechanism is ubiquitous in small molecule photoredox catalysis,26,27

121 photoenzymes are relatively rare, with only three currently known in nature. The oldest

122 photoenzyme is DNA photolyase, a flavin-dependent enzyme responsible for repairing

123 pyrimidine cyclobutane dimers in DNA.18 These dimeric lesions are formed when DNA is

124 irradiated with UV light. In this enzyme, the reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor

125 (FADhq–) serves as the photocatalyst, initially reducing the pyrimidine dimer to initiate a retro 2+2

126 reaction followed by oxidation of the resulting radical anion by FAD semiquinone (FADsq).28,29

127 Many homologs of this enzyme have additional deazaflavin or pterin cofactors to expand the

128 wavelengths of light that can promote this reactivity. Another well-studied natural photoenzyme

129 is light-dependent protochlorophyllide reductase (LPOR), a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide

130 phosphate (NADPH) dependent enzyme responsible for reducing protochlorophyllide (PChlide)

131 to chlorophyllide.30 Among natural photoenzymes, LPOR remains unique in that the reduction.

132 occurs via photoexcitation of the PChlide substrate rather than the NADPH cofactor. This excited

133 state can oxidize NADPH via single electron transfer to form NADPH+. and PChlide radical anion.

134 Proton transfer from a conserved tyrosine and hydrogen atom abstraction from NADPH+.


<!-- Page 7 -->


135 produces the product. As these enzymes hold little value to synthetic chemists and have been

136 recently reviewed, we will not elaborate on their function or mechanism in this review.

137 2.1 Fatty Acid Photodecarboxylase

138 The third natural photoenzyme is Fatty Acid Photodecarboxylase (FAP). As reported in

139 2017  by  Beisson  and  coworkers,  this  is  a  natural  photoenzyme  that  catalyzes  the

140 hydrodecarboxylation of fatty acids, a reaction with potential synthetic value (Figure 2Erreur !

141 Source du renvoi introuvable.A).31 In contrast to previously known fatty acid decarboxylases,

142 which catalyze oxidative decarboxylation to afford a terminal alkene, FAPs facilitate a redox-

143 neutral reaction to form an alkane.32,33 The first member of this family was found in the microalgae

144 Chlorella variabilis NC64A (EC 4.1.1.106), although putative FAPs are found in many algal

145 species suggesting this enzyme family in ancient.34 This flavoprotein is in the glucose-methanol-

146 choline (GMC) family of oxidoreductases. Like other GMC oxidoreductases, FAP is a two-domain

147 protein where the first domain contains the N-terminal residues and is responsible for flavin

148 binding and stabilization, while the second domain is involved in substrate and product binding

149 and trafficking.31 The conserved residues in the FAD binding domain interact with the FAD

150 cofactor, causing it to adopt a bent “butterfly” conformation 14º degrees from planarity. This

151 structural feature red-shifts the ground state FAD absorption spectrum which could aid in light

152 absorption.35

153 2.1.1 Reaction Mechanism and Substrate Scope

154 Mechanistically, the reaction begins with the carboxylic acid binding close to the FAD

155 cofactor within the protein active site (Figure 2Erreur ! Source du renvoi introuvable.B).

156 Photoexcitation of the FAD cofactor with visible light (λ=325-530 nm with λmax=467 nm) affords

157 the singlet excited state 1FAD* (Figure 2BErreur ! Source du renvoi introuvable., step 1), which

158 rapidly oxidizes the carboxylate (~300 ps) and, upon decarboxylation, affords an alkyl radical and

159 FAD●– (Figure 2Erreur ! Source du renvoi introuvable.B, step 2). The quantum efficiency of this

160 step is 80%, indicating that decarboxylation is favored by comparison to back-electron transfer.

161 Radical termination occurs to provide a red-shifted FAD intermediate attributed to the cofactor

2.1.2 Reaction Condition Engineering

198 Recently, two studies reported immobilizing fatty acid photodecarboxylase with the goal of

199 increasing its stability and activity. Chanquia et al. tested the activity of CvFAP on EziG® beads

200 containing Fe(III) cations for His-tag affinity immobilization.39 They found the Amber carrier to

201 give the highest degree of immobilization (84%) and to provide 2.8% yield when decarboxylating

202 C17 carboxylic acids. The immobilized enzyme could be reused up to three times in aqueous

203 media. In this study, they also explored the impact that deep eutectic solvents have on FAP

204 activity. When immobilized, deep eutectic solvents diminish reusability. However, when not

205 immobilized, the mixture 30% Choline chloride and glycerol in water provides a nearly 20%

206 increase in conversion by comparison to water alone, suggesting the eutectic solvents can

207 modulate activity.

208 In another study, Simić et al. developed a strategy for running CvFAP in continuous flow.40

209 The authors carefully studied different parameters such as a) carrier selection for immobilization

210 and to limit enzyme leaching during the reaction, b) Light condition: intensity, wavelength and

211 light penetration, c) Substrate solubility and d) illumination conditions coupled to residence time

212 for maximizing the production. They found that immobilization of CvFAP on EziG® Opal provided

213 the highest conversions. However, this strategy was incompatible with the continuous flow setup.

214 Consequently, moving to a system with Ammoeng 102 as a surfactant to increase the solubility

215 of palmitic acid in Tris buffer and optimizing other reaction parameters, the authors report a

216 space time yield of 5.7 g.l-1h-1 for the production of pentadecane, that is the highest productivity

217 of CvFAP report to date.

218 Hollmann and coworkers found FAP decarboxylation activity on short and medium carboxylic

219 acids (C1-C6) could be enhanced by adding simple alkanes, ranging in size from nonane to

220 pentadecane, as molecular decoys (Figure 4A).41 For instance, nearly six times as much methane

221 can be generated from acetic acid using CvFAP with pentadecane as a molecular decoy. The

222 general strategy was successful across C1 to C6 substrates. This strategy also broadened the


<!-- Page 11 -->


223 scope to include unsaturated fatty acids (e.g., acrylic acid, propiolic acid) and short alkyl chains

224 (e.g., propionic acid). Additionally, CvFAP catalyzed the decarboxylation of formic acid, releasing

225 H2 (Figure 4A).

226 The authors hypothesize that adding a decoy molecule induces the same conformational

227 changes that occur when longer fatty acids bind to the protein, helping to activate the enzyme

228 for photoexcitation. A kinetic study of 13CH3−CO2H decarboxylation supports this hypothesis to

229 form 13CH4. In this study, the authors found that the reaction rate was only dependent on acetic

230 acid concentration, indicating that the additive does not facilitate substrate binding but instead

231 activates the enzyme for new photoinduced electron transfer. While primary radicals are

232 terminated using the mechanism outlined above, Hollmann proposes a different means of

233 termination for unstable methyl radical. DFT calculations suggest that radical termination occurs

234 via alkylation of FAD●– to form a covalent dearomatized methyl quinone flavin adduct, which

235 upon protonation, forms methane and oxidized FAD quinone (Figure 4B).

456 Nicotinamide-dependent ketoreductases (KREDs) are widely used in chemical production for

457 the enantioselective reduction of ketones to alcohols.61 Their NADH or NADPH cofactors act as

468 NADH or NADPH radical cation delivers a hydrogen atom selectively to one face of the prochiral

469 𝛼-acyl radical, providing the corresponding dehalogenated product. NAD+ or NADP+ is then

502 Flavin-dependent' ene’-reductases (EREDs) are a class of biocatalysts frequently used in

503 organic synthesis. This enzyme family, referred to as old yellow enzymes (OYEs), was initially

504 discovered in brewer's bottom yeast (Saccharomyces pastorianus) in 1932 and is thought to be

505 expressed in response to oxidative stress.66,67 Subsequent studies revealed OYE homologs in all

506 domains of life, with members found in natural product pathways and RNA modification.68,69

507 Traditionally, OYEs are used for the stereoselective reduction of activated alkenes and provide

508 chiral products with high levels of stereoselectivity. This reduction occurs via a hydride transfer

509 from FMN hydroquinone (FMNhq) to the electrophilic 𝛽-position to afford FMN quinone and an

510 enzyme-bound enolate, which is protonated by a conserved tyrosine. NAD(P)H can reduce FMN

511 back to the FMNhq in a ping-pong mechanism.70,71 These enzymes reduce alkenes with trans

512 selectivity, making them complementary to traditional metal-catalyzed hydrogenations (Figure

513 13).72

514 In the initial characterization of OYE1, Massey found that when photochemically reduced,

515 OYE1 can kinetically and thermodynamically stabilize the anionic flavin semiquinone (FMNsq).73

516 While unrealized at the time, the ability of the protein to stabilize open-shell flavin oxidation

517 states opens the door to EREDs catalyzing radical reactions. In one possible scenario, FMNhq

518 could serve as a single electron reductant (FMNhq/FMNsq = -230mV vs. SCE) of an organic

519 substrate.74 The resulting substrate-centered radicals could be terminated via hydrogen atom

520 transfer from the FMNsq (BDEcalc = 59 kcal/mol).75

2.5 Photoenzymes Using Non-Natural Cofactors and Amino Acids

886 In contrast to the breadth of work on expanding the natural reactivity of enzyme cofactors

887 with light irradiation, there has been relatively little progress on photoinitiated transformations

888 via a covalently linked chromophore. Introducing non-natural cofactors opens the door to

889 accessing reactivities that are inaccessible to chromophores in nature. Green and coworkers

890 recently reported a designed enzyme for enantioselective [2+2]-cycloadditions enabled by a

891 non-canonical 4-benzoyl-phenylalanine (BpA) residue.97 The authors selected a computationally

892 designed Diels-Alderase (DA_20_00) as the starting scaffold because of the mechanistic

893 similarities between thermal [4+2]-cycloadditions and photochemical [2+2] reactions.98 The

894 authors introduced the BpA residue at position 173 in the active site of a computationally

895 designed Diels-Alderase to generate the enzyme EnT1.0. Irradiation with 365 and 395 nm LEDs

896 promoted triplet energy transfer (EnT) photocatalysis between the BpA residue and substrate,

897 enabling the [2+2] cycloaddition in modest yield, regioselectivity, and enantioselectivity.

898 Over the course of three rounds of directed evolution, the optimized photoenzyme

899 EnT1.3 could catalyze the intramolecular [2+2] cycloaddition of a variety of quinolones bearing

900 a pendant alkene with quantitative conversion and up to 99.5:0.5 e.r. (Figure 29A). A crystal

901 structure of the evolved biocatalyst with the quinolone product bound revel substrate π-stacking

902 interactions between both the BpA173 and H287 sidechains crucial for effective triplet energy

903 transfer. The crystal structure also revealed hydrogen bonding interactions between the

904 quinolone product and Y121 and Q195 postulated to be important for substrate orientation and

905 activity. Indeed, the Y121F or Q195A mutations result in reduced yield and enantioselectivity

906 (Figure 29B). In contrast to versions of this reaction catalyzed by small molecule catalysts, this

907 reaction is not sensitive to O2, suggesting that the protein environment is protecting the

908 benzophenone amino acid from O2 and limiting the formation of singlet oxygen.

960 3.0 Synergistic Photoenzymatic Catalysis 961

962 Synergistic photoenzymatic catalysis describes enzymatic transformations where the

963 enzymatic mechanism for converting starting material to product involves electron or energy

964 transfer  from  an  exogenous  photocatalyst.  This  family  of  reactivity  is  distinct  from

965 photobiocatalytic systems for cofactor turnover because the electron transfer event involving the

966 photocatalyst is essential for the biocatalytic mechanism for converting starting material to

967 product.

968 3.1 Synergistic Reactions Involving Native Reactivity

969 3.1.1 Cytochromes P450 970

971 Cytochrome P450s are powerful catalysts for the asymmetric and regioselective

972 hydroxylation of unactivated C–H bonds using molecular oxygen and a reductant. These proteins

973 require a heme domain for oxygen activation and hydroxylation and a reductase domain to

974 deliver electrons from NADPH to the heme domain for catalysis (via flavin mediators). The most

975 widely used cytochrome P450 for biocatalytic transformations is P450BM3, a catalyst that has the

976 reductase domain covalently linked to the heme domain.104 Fundamental studies by Gray and

977 others demonstrated how electrons travel through proteins. In these studies, small molecule

978 photocatalysts were often used to initiate electron transfer events. 105,106 Building on these

979 studies, Cheruzel and coworkers demonstrated the heme domain of P450BM3 bioconjugated with

980 polypyridyl ruthenium photocatalysts can facilitate the C–H hydroxylation without requiring the

981 traditional NADPH reductant. 107 Ru(bpy)2(phenA)Cl2 was linked to the heme domain via cysteine

982 bioconjugation to P450BM3-L407C; a variant containing cysteine that can react with the mutant

983 via the iodoacetamide functional handle on the phenIA ligand. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the

984 location of photocatalyst bioconjugation plays an important role in the efficiency of the strategy,

985 with other positions providing lower yields and total turnover numbers. 108,109 To improve the

986 driving force of electron transfer, the 2,2’-bipyridine (bpy) ligands were substituted to 4,4’-


<!-- Page 50 -->


987 dimethoxy-2,2’-bipyridine ligand resulting in an 80 mV decrease in reduction potential. The

988 authors  proposed  the  following  mechanism  for  this  non-natural  system  (Figure  33).

989 Photoexcitation of the Ruthenium photocatalyst provides an excited state that is reductively

990 quenched by Sodium diethyldithiocarbamate (DTC) to provide a long-lived Ru(I) state, which

991 supplies the electrons required for hydroxylation.

992 While total turnover numbers (TTNs) could not be compared to the native holoenzyme, initial

993 rates of product formation are roughly an order of magnitude lower. However, when compared

994 to other reduction strategies, such as electrochemical reduction or photochemical reactions with

995 deazaflavin, this synergistic approach performs favorably (Figure 33A). The P450BM3 enzymes

996 were also demonstrated to regioselectively hydroxylate the allylic position of 10-undecenoic acid

997 in 40% yield and 92.5:7.5 e.r. (Figure 33b).110 In subsequent studies, Cheruzel applied this system

998 to the benzylic hydroxylation of trifluoromethylated substrates.111 In this reaction, the authors

999 used a photoredox reaction developed by Stephenson et al. to trifluoromethylate aromatic rings

1000 with alkyl substituents to form trifluoromethylated products with various regioselectivities.112

1001 Next, they used the P450BM3  photocatalyst hybrid to hydroxylate the benzylic position.

1002 Interestingly, in cases where the trifluoromethylation protocol produced a mixture of para, meta,

1003 and ortho-isomers, the subsequent hydroxylation would occur preferentially on one product,

1004 indicating that steric and electronic properties of the substrate strongly influence its reactivity in

1005 the hydroxylation reaction. Moreover, the authors found that mutations within the protein active

1006 site could influence the selectivity of the hydroxylation step.

The Hyster group demonstrated the viability of this general synergistic strategy in a

radical deacetoxylation of 𝛼-acetoxyketones using nicotinamide-dependent double-bond

deacetoxylation reactions in the dark or with blue or green LEDs. However, upon the addition of

Bengal as a photocatalyst, where the desired product was formed in 87% yield with 93:7 er.120 In

solution, the xanthene dye Rose Bengal (E1/2 red [RB/ RB•–]=-0.99V vs. SCE)121 is incapable of

reducing the model ketone (Ep/2 red =-1.30V vs. SCE). However, enzymatic binding of the ketone

substrate attenuates its redox potential, making it accessible to RB•– reduction only within the

enzyme active site. Based on the native reaction mechanism, the authors propose that a tyrosine

hydrogen bonds to the carbonyl of the substrate, providing 170 mV of electronic activation and

thus providing a thermodynamic preference for reduction within the protein active site. Upon

reduction of the starting material, the resulting ketyl radical undergoes a spin-center shift to

eliminate acetate and form an enzyme-bound -acyl radical, which can subsequently be

terminated via enantioselective HAT from enzyme-bound NADPH. Isotopic labeling experiments

support the hypothesis that nicotinamide functions as the source of hydrogen atom (Figure 37).

1171 4.0 Photobiocatalytic Cascades

1172 Photobiocatalytic  cascades  are  biocatalytic  transformations  where  an  enzyme  and

1173 photocatalyst are present in a reaction, but the photocatalyst is not involved in the electron

1174 transfer events required to convert the starting material to product. In this scenario, the

1175 photocatalyst is operating entirely independently of the enzyme. The most common variant of

1176 this cascade strategy is cofactor reduction by the photocatalyst or in situ generation of peroxide.

1177 More recently, research has been focused on organic transformations that can be run in the

1178 presence of enzymes for dynamic kinetic resolutions. This section is organized based on the role

1179 of the photocatalyst in the reaction.

1517 4.2 Photobiocatalytic Cascades 1518

1519 In the previous section, the photocatalysts were functioning on a cofactor, catalyst, or

1520 substrate to generate an intermediate required for the enzymatic reaction. In this section, we will

1521 focus on photocatalytic reactions that modify the substrate with which the enzyme reacts. This

1522 family of reactivity falls into two basic categories; i) reactions where the enzymatic and

1523 photochemical reactions occur simultaneously (one-pot/one-step reactions), and ii) reactions

1524 where the enzymatic and photochemical reactions occur in separate steps (one-pot/two-step

1525 reactions).

1526 4.2.1 One-Pot/One-Step Photobiocatalytic Cascades

1527 Photoredox catalysts generate radical intermediates under mild conditions and are

1528 compatible with thermally sensitive proteins. Moreover, in contrast to thermal radical initiators

1529 that can only generate a single radical chain, photoredox catalysts can initiate multiple radical

1530 chains and rescue intermediates that fall into unproductive pathways. These features make

1531 photoredox catalysts well-suited for facilitating racemization in dynamic kinetic resolutions. In

1532 pioneering studies, Bertrand and Gil found that lipases can participate in dynamic kinetic


<!-- Page 78 -->


1533 resolutions of amines when using thiyl radicals as reagents for substrate racemization.172,173,174,175

1534 In many of their studies, thiyl radical formation was initiated AIBN. As this initiator decomposed

1535 over time, multiple recharges of AIBN were required to achieve high yield and selectivity.

1536 Zhou and co-workers explored the same type of dynamic kinetic resolution using

1537 Ir(ppy)2(dtbbpy)PF6 as a photocatalyst for radical initiation and mercaptooctanol as a hydrogen

1538 atom transfer catalyst for racemization of the amine substrate (Figure 56).176 Mechanistically,

1539 racemization occurred via oxidation and deprotonation of mercaptooctanol to afford a thiyl

1540 radical that will selectively abstract the 𝛼-amino hydrogen atom of the substrate to afford the 𝛼-

1582 Biocatalytic transformations have been shown to have good compatibility in the presence

1583 of chemocatalytic methods in synergistic, dynamic one-pot reactions. However, many examples

1584 of chemoenzymatic catalysis comprise dynamic kinetic resolutions that typically involve the

1585 racemization of dynamic (i.e., chemically active) C–H stereocenters (e.g., -keto, -amino). In a

1586 collaboration between the Hyster and MacMillan groups, a strategy was developed to target

1587 traditionally static stereocenters and render them dynamic in a stereoconvergent transformation

1588 (Figure 59).180 They developed a novel racemization targeting traditionally static -keto C–H

1589 stereocenter racemization, a method lacking generality due to its inert nature. However, this

1590 racemization could be realized through a merger of photoredox, organo-, and hydrogen atom

1591 transfer (HAT) catalysis.181  Mechanistically, the racemization operates through the initial

1592 condensation of an amine organocatalyst with a -stereogenic ketone substrate to form the

1593 corresponding enamine intermediate. Oxidation of this intermediate via an excited state iridium

1594 photoredox catalyst forms an enaminyl radical cation with a substantially acidified  position.

1595 Deprotonation at this position forms a key stereoablated -enaminyl radical species, which can

1596 then undergo achiral HAT with a thiol HAT catalyst. The resulting racemic enamine can then

1597 undergo hydrolysis to the racemic ketone. Finally, thiyl reduction by the reduced photoredox

1598 catalyst followed by protonation completes the photoredox and HAT catalytic cycles. As this

1599 racemization occurs, a kinetic resolution mediated by a ketoreductase forms enantio- and

1600 diastereoenriched 3-substituted alcohol products. In the optimization of this complex process, it

1601 was important that the amine organocatalyst was hydrophobic to outcompete enamine

1602 hydrolysis in aqueous conditions as well as to mitigate enzyme deactivation.

1673 5.0 Whole-Cell Photobiocatalytic Reactions Using Cyanobacteria 1674

1675 Oxidoreductases, such as alcohol dehydrogenases, ene-reductases, amine

1676 dehydrogenases, and oxygenases, are among the most widely used enzymes in organic

1677 synthesis.185 All these reactions require stoichiometric amounts of reductants such as glucose,

1678 formate, or 2-propanol, and form equimolar amounts of byproduct, gluconic acid, CO2, and

1679 acetone, respectively, during the processes.186 The poor atom efficiency of cofactor regeneration

1680 systems becomes one of the main bottlenecks for the application of these enzymes on an

1681 industrial scale. To solve this problem, a strategy that couples the enzymatic redox processes to

1682 the photosystem in photosynthetic cells has recently been developed. In these reactions, the

1683 cyanobacteria produce NADPH in a water oxidation reaction. These reducing equivalents can be

1684 used by biocatalysts to facilitate transformations.187 This section will be organized based on how

1685 the biocatalyst interfaces with the cyanobacterium. In the first section, we will focus on systems

1686 that use enzymes natively expressed by the cyanobacterium. The second section will focus on

1687 cyanobacterium heterologously expressing a biocatalyst. The final section will focus on reactions

1688 where reducing equivalents are shuttled across the cyanobacterium membrane to enable

1689 biocatalytic transformations outside the cell.

1844 5.3 Transmembrane Shuttling

1845 Winkler and Kroutil recognized that heterologous expression and substrate transport across

1846 the cyanobacteria wall presented a challenge in more broadly implementing photosynthetic

1847 organisms in biocatalytic reactions. To overcome this issue, they developed a shuttling strategy

1848 where acetone would shuttle reducing equivalents from a cyanobacterium to biocatalysts in

1849 solution.209 A cyanobacterium (Synechocystis sp. PC6803) heterologously expressing the alcohol

1850 dehydrogenase from Lactobacillus kefir (Lk-ADH) reduces acetone to i-PrOH using

1851 photosynthetically produced NADPH (Module A). After passing through the cell membrane, i-

1852 PrOH is oxidized by the Lk-ADH to produce NADPH (Module B), which can be used by the

1853 enzyme of interest to modify a substrate (Module C). This approach is highly modular, enabling

1854 a single cyanobacterium to drive many different types of biocatalytic reactions without requiring

1855 the cyanobacterium to express the biocatalyst of interest. In the initial report, the authors focus

1856 on systems where an ‘ene’-reductase serves as module C. They also demonstrate that alcohol

1857 dehydrogenases, imine reductases, and Baeyer-Villiger Monooxygenases can serve as module

1858 C (Figure 73).

The term “photobiocatalysis” has been recently coined to broadly describe the combination

of light and enzymes for use in synthetic organic chemistry. The field has blossomed

exponentially to the point where key mechanistic differences have begun to surface, the most

significant of which is the role of light in the transformation. The goal of this review, therefore, is

to characterize and thoroughly describe and delineate the roles of light in this new field. We

have defined three key terms: photoenzymatic catalysis, synergistic photoenzymatic catalysis,

1873 We have shown that photoenzymatic catalysis, the direct excitation of the enzyme cofactor,

1874 although initially harnessed by nature in one form as fatty acid photodecarboxylase, which has

1875 been successfully exploited for its synthetic capabilities (Section 2.1), has primarily been

1876 accessed to facilitate new, non-native enzymatic transformations. The excitation of nicotinamide-

1877 (Section 2.2) and flavin-based (Section 2.3) cofactors for the creation and manipulation of open

1878 shell reactive intermediates has been found to be a general strategy for C – H and C – C bond

1879 formations, as well as radical polymerizations. The extension of photoenzymatic chemistry to

1880 include the incorporation and excitation of non-canonical cofactors has also been explored

1881 (Section 2.4).

1882 We have also described the term synergistic photoenzymatic chemistry as the use of light to

1883 excite an exogenous photocatalyst that can then perform energy or electron transfer to the

1884 enzyme cofactor to carry out the desired transformation. We have shown that this regime can be

1885 used to facilitate both native (Section 3.1) and non-native reactions (Section 3.2). This reactivity

1886 is distinct from photobiocatalysis, for which light-mediated chemistry is not directly part of the

1887 conversion of starting material to product but rather, is used to generate another essential

1888 component of the reaction, independent of the action of the enzyme. In the realm of

1889 photobiocatalysis, light is used primarily for the generation of active enzyme cofactors (Section

1890 4.1) but has recently become particularly popular for the generation of enzyme-active

1891 intermediates in dynamic kinetic resolutions and chemoenzymatic cascades (Section 4.2). Finally,

1892 we show the use of whole-cell cyanobacteria to facilitate light-driven cofactor regeneration

1893 through the manipulation of the cell’s native redox processes (Section 5).

1894 We hope that the review clarifies and distinguishes between the multiple modes of

1895 combining light and enzymes for use in organic synthesis. As new examples emerged, the

1896 nuances of the described works necessitated that these new terms be developed to fully

1897 understand and appreciate the mechanistic details of each transformation. We hope that this

## Abstract

Victoria Harbour waterfront development faces challenges in the relationships among private and public stakeholders and developers. Six waterfront cities determined to be successful were benchmarked against Hong Kong and then studied in depth. We gathered the guidelines, laws, projects, ownership, and physical status of the waterfronts from Baltimore, Maryland, Chicago, Illinois, New York City, New York, Singapore, Republic of Singapore, Sydney, Australia, and Vancouver, Canada. We used these examples to draft conclusions on the elements that make a successful waterfront, how to achieve unity of a waterfront, and the role of guidelines in waterfront development and presented them to Designing Hong Kong.

## Executive Summary

The Victoria Harbour waterfront area is currently not satisfying the needs of both the public and private sectors on the promenade. The purpose of our project was to provide conclusions on how other successful waterfronts have worked with the integration of private and public sectors in order for the Victoria Harbour waterfront to apply what other waterfront cities have learned. Our first objective was to identify and compare the most successful waterfront characteristics, specifically the design and makeup of waterfronts, in the selected cities. Then, we identified the laws and regulations surrounding waterfront development, specifically in regard to the construction and operation of private businesses along waterfronts. Our final objective was to identify the most successful ways to integrate public and private sector stakeholders based on how other cities had done this. To begin our analysis, we first found which waterfronts around the world are considered the best. We researched popular waterfronts around the world through tourism and news sites. From that we compiled a list of the cities that appeared most frequently in the lists and compared them to the climate, property type, and geography of Hong Kong in order to compile the final six cities for intensive study. The selected cities were Baltimore, Chicago, New York City, Singapore, Sydney, and Vancouver. These six cities all qualify as having some of the best waterfronts in the world and are all similar to Hong Kong. By learning about these waterfronts in depth, we were able to make useful conclusions about waterfronts so Victoria Harbour may improve theirs.

We conducted archival research as our main method for all of the six cities selected. We conducted literature research on each of the six cities’ waterfront’s history, the ownership of waterfront property, funding of waterfront development and management, who the developers of the waterfront were, what kind of developments were allowed, the guidelines and zoning laws in place, and the actual physical status of the waterfront. To further research on geographical characteristics of the cities’ waterfronts, we looked at satellite images via Google Earth and Google Maps. We also conducted several semi-structured interviews in which we gathered information on the developmental process of each city waterfront. We sent out a survey for people who had visited one or more of the selected waterfronts to complete in order to gather information on what people enjoyed about them.

We have found several elements of a waterfront that need to be present in order for it to be deemed successful. These can be broken up into three main components: the environmental focus, having a variety of developments along the waterfront, and a pleasant atmosphere. Designers should put in place plans that will contribute towards a resilient waterfront that can withstand rising sea levels, erosion, and other effects of climate change. There needs to be a variety of developments along the waterfront, because only having open or green spaces is not enough to attract and continue to attract people. The waterfront should also create a special experience and atmosphere that people are able to immerse themselves into and establish an emotional connection to. This connection is what will encourage them to come back.

In order to achieve a unified waterfront, the stakeholders and planners should have a clear idea of who the waterfront is being developed for. Once the needs of that population are clear the plans must be adjusted to include those as well as: accessibility, such as public transportation, visibility of the water, community engagement such as a variety of cultural activities, and community incentive such as promotion of and a space for local businesses. A way of making sure these needs are met is to include the community surrounding the development in the initial planning stages of the development. A multi-step review process for the communication between the community, the stakeholders, and any other development experts involved must be conducted in order to ensure thorough analysis. This review process is a cyclical process of feedback between all entities.

We found that each city has their own structure when it comes to development on waterfront land. In many cities, there are a number of stakeholders that develop on the waterfront. In any successful waterfront, there must be cooperation between the stakeholders so different sections of the waterfront can be well-incorporated with each other. We found that developmental guidelines are the main method of ensuring the unity of the waterfront is followed by the developers. ## 1. Introduction

For over 2,000 years, harbors have been used as venues for the exchange of goods and passengers between boats and the shore (National Geographic Society, 2011). They allow for communities around the world to trade with each other, so easy access to them is essential for a city to have a smoothly running economy. Economic factors first attracted merchants to the waterfront but as time went on people began gathering at them for recreational purposes, such as strolling by the water or looking out at magnificent ships coming in. The waterfronts began benefitting both the city and country’s economy but also the people who lived there in other ways. Hong Kong’s harbor, the Victoria Harbor, has been a critical part of the city since the early 1840s (Summers, 2019). During that time the city’s rule was handed over to the British Empire, which relied on it as a major trading center for obtaining Chinese goods such as spices, tea, ceramics, and silk. The harbor remained an important part of Hong Kong’s economy as the colony grew to be a global leader in maritime trade. In attempts to keep up with its economic growth, the government began to reclaim land to create more space for development. That land was leased out to many private developers who constructed highrise buildings along the waterfront, which often blocked access to the waterfront for the public. Designing Hong Kong (DHK) (2020), a non-profit organization promoting sustainable urban planning in Hong Kong, has spent years developing projects to achieve a well-developed and ‘beautiful’ harbor. A study conducted by Cyrus Wong (2020) and sponsored by DHK, identified a series of criteria to assess the range of strengths and weaknesses of each section of the waterfront. This study provides a framework for comparing and contrasting Victoria Harbour’s waterfront with those in other cities, which we found to be successful. They have better developed their waterfronts to get beyond their economic functions and serve as places to socialize, relax, exercise, eat and be entertained. Waterfront development is an ongoing task that requires extensive planning. DHK has been working diligently to help improve the waterfront design plans while also working with the Hong Kong government. However, there is still more planning to be done in order to create a space that people can enjoy, find easy access, and find attractive and safe, and yet also contribute to Hong Kong’s economy. The purpose of our project was to determine how waterfront cities around the world have dealt with the challenge of making their waterfronts accessible, attractive, enjoyable and financially sustainable so that Victoria Harbour’s waterfront can learn from their successes and avoid any mistakes they may have made. Our first objective was to identify and compare the most successful characteristics, specifically the design and makeup of waterfronts, in the selected cities. ### 2.1 Importance of Waterfronts

Waterfront areas are important to port cities all around the world. They aid in economic growth, boost urban water resources and improve people’s lives (Chai, n.d.). Access to bodies of water such as oceans, seas, lakes or rivers, has been essential to the establishment of many large and successful cities (Hradilova, 2012).

Post-Industrial Revolution, many cities began to deindustrialize (Conlon, 2017). The once booming trading centers were left with abandoned warehouses and unused waterfronts. In the past several decades, communities and governments have come together to revive these mismanaged areas. Not only were they unpleasant to look at, but there was also an increasing need for urban green spaces within cities (Dobson et al., 2021).

The connection between cities and nature became increasingly important to residents in the cities (Hradilova, 2012). Nature is where the people are able to escape the commotion of the city and find serenity. According to Dobson et al. (2021), many studies show that there is a strong connection between good mental health and well-being and access to nature. The creation and maintenance of urban green spaces can significantly improve a city population’s well-being. These green spaces include most areas of nature, like parks and access to water. Cities around the world have been working hard to bring back life to their waterfronts and create open spaces that attract people with their accessibility, activities, and spatial arrangements (Hradilova, 2012). One of these cities is Hong Kong.

### 2.2 Hong Kong

Hong Kong is a bustling region located in the southeastern part of China at the end of the Guangdong Peninsula. It is made up of three sections: Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, and the New Territories (Wong, 2016). It served as an essential trade center for China by connecting its economy and goods to the rest of the world (Encyclopedia.com, 2020).

Today, Hong Kong is the seventh largest city in the world by GDP (GlobalData, 2019). As one of the main attractions in Hong Kong, the Victoria Harbour waterfront is vital for bringing in tourists who spend around $40 billion dollars each year in Hong Kong (Hong Kong


<!-- Page 14 -->


4

Tourism Statistics 1995-2021, 2021). However, Victoria Harbour’s waterfront is not operating for everyone’s benefit because of private developers’ battles over the rights of using public space for commercial purposes, compromising the walkability and accessibility of the space. This is partially due to the money driven mindset of both developers and the government in Hong Kong (P. Zimmerman, video chats, 2021). The government makes their money from leasing land out to developers and charging a premium for sought after land, on which they can make luxury waterfront apartments, or hotels with private patios, which both limit the public’s  accessibility of the space. There are limited guidelines that define the type of developments allowed on the waterfront, the amount of open space necessary, or maintaining accessible areas along it. This makes it especially difficult for the space to cater to the majority of the people who live and visit in the city. These issues can be better addressed now since land reclamation in Hong Kong has stopped.

Hong Kong is an ambitious city and has sought to expand its reach and accelerate its growth through land reclamation between 1877 and 2020 (Tristan Justin Bove NG, 2020). Land reclamation projects in Victoria Harbour made it very difficult to develop and maintain a consistently attractive waterfront due to the fact that their shoreline had been constantly changing (Skala, 2007). Over 143 years, 70 km2 of land reclamation has taken place in Hong Kong. This equates to their shoreline changing by several meters every year, making it extremely difficult to manage a single waterfront district since the bounds for the waterfront were not defined. However, since 1997, Hong Kong has classified Victoria Harbour as a public asset in the Protection of the Harbour Ordinance Bill, limiting land reclamation activities that may damage it. In 2004, the Court of Final Appeal finally blocked the Town Planning Board from approving any development that called for land reclamation in Victoria Harbour. Since that ordinance went into effect, DHK and a number of other non-profit organizations, such as the Harbour Business Forum, have been searching for ways to improve Victoria Harbour and turn it into a more appealing space for everyone (Design HK Harbour District, n.d.).

An indication of this would be shops with a glass panel and roman blinds within them to allow a flexible visual interaction. ## 5. Our Conclusions

In this chapter we will present the conclusions we have arrived at from our research. We will outline the elements of a successful waterfront, how to achieve a unified waterfront, and how laws and regulations should be issued in order to ensure a waterfront is well-connected and accessible by all.

### 5.1 Elements of a Successful Waterfronts

We have found several waterfront elements of a waterfront that need to be present in order for it to be successful. These can be broken up into three main components: the environmental focus, having a variety of developments along the waterfront, and a pleasant atmosphere.

5.1.1 Environmental Focus

In order for a waterfront to be successful, the designing process must focus on environmental factors. Specifically, designers should put plans in place that will contribute towards a resilient waterfront that can withstand rising sea levels, erosion, and other effects of climate change. Our research shows that members of waterfront planning committees tend to assess the development’s commitment to preserving the surrounding ecology and its ability to withstand future natural waterfront damage. They do so while delegating the city funds because they will not budget for a waterfront that might fall apart in the future. In order for a waterfront to thrive, be accessible, and bring in traffic, it has to withstand deterioration and climate change. After the environmental aspects are considered, the developers should continue with the rest of the waterfront planning.

5.1.2 Variety of Features

There needs to be a variety of developments along the waterfront. Merely having open or green spaces is not enough to attract people. These various developments include entertainment venues, sports fields, amusement attractions, convention centers, shops, restaurants, museums and more. These options and establishments provide a diverse collection of activities waterfront visitors can participate in. They contribute to promoting the city’s culture and its atmosphere. These features benefit both the public and the private sectors. People are able to visit the attractions and spend more time at the waterfront. Visitors will benefit the private developer stakeholders by bringing in cash flow to the local restaurants, shops, and other attractions. In addition, people tend to attract more people. They are naturally interested in areas that other people are also visiting, so the more people who visit, the more business local shops, restaurants and other venues will get and the more attractive that area will be for real estate investment.

It is important to note that these attractions must be well integrated into the waterfront as a whole. Each venue should have a clear view of the water, whether it be through large glass


<!-- Page 53 -->


| businesses in the area as they will drive traffic to the waterfront. | These elements appeal to locals |  |
|---|---|---|
| because they provide an alternative to the dense urban environment of a city. |  | A way of making |

windows or open entrances, and having seats facing the harbour. They should be easily accessible from both the street and the waterfront promenade.

5.1.3 Waterfront Atmosphere

Generally, people come to a waterfront area because they enjoy its ambiance. People enjoy spending time around others in areas that promote a sense of community and safety. Designing a welcoming space for all is essential to the success of a waterfront.

Incorporating the history of the area where the waterfront is developed is one way to establish a nostalgic mood. Incorporating old and refurbished industrial buildings can bring people back to times when the waterfront served as a port and was an essential component of the city’s economy. The waterfront should create a special experience and atmosphere that people are able to immerse themselves into and establish an emotional connection to. This connection is what will keep them coming back.

### 5.2 Achieving a Unified Waterfront

In order for a waterfront to be successful, there needs to be a comprehensive plan which views the waterfront holistically. The goals of the waterfront should be agreed upon in the initial design process and closely followed throughout the rest of the development. A clear and concise development plan should take into consideration the target audience, their needs, and their preferences for the future of the space.

5.2.1 Population the waterfront is being designed for

We found that it is key for the developing group(s) to have a clear vision of who the waterfront is being designed for and the purpose the area will serve for this audience. The initial purpose of some successful waterfronts studied, was to engage locals surrounding the area. These individuals are of all ages and of different backgrounds, so their diverse input should be sought after. This will result in more local engagement with the designated area. It also lowers the chances of near-by communities getting upset over disruptions in their daily lives, such as noise or large buildings blocking their views. Designs that cater to communities nearby must include: high accessibility, such as multiple entrances to the park and a connection to the city’s public transportation, visibility of the water, and an area for the community to congregate and participate in a variety of cultural activities. There should also be encouragement for local businesses in the area as they will drive traffic to the waterfront. These elements appeal to locals because they provide an alternative to the dense urban environment of a city. A way of making sure these needs are met is to include the community surrounding the development in planning the initial steps of development and allow for input and suggestions. This will result in an establishment built for the people and by the people.

Our research also shows that waterfront attractions often appeal to tourists. They often visit areas that have a large variety of activities, such as museums, amusement parks, and large


<!-- Page 54 -->


44

venues with concerts or sports games. These attractions are lively and exciting. Tourists are also willing to pay more for larger activities in contrast to locals. We credit this to tourists looking for a local experience from the city they are visiting. Whoever the designated population is, whether locals or tourists, there must be a thorough process of identifying their needs and an analysis of the desired outcomes of the experience being provided by the waterfront area.

5.2.2 Multi-Step Review Process

In order to carry out a thorough and complete plan of the waterfront, there must be a specific and detailed review process of the planned design. Aside from the community input, it is important to have personnel knowledgeable in each of the areas mentioned in the previous section and for them to give input for the development. All personnel must act consistently in viewing and designing the waterfront as a whole. This means having a holistic perspective that takes into consideration all parts of the waterfront, not just sections of it. Once the target population and location of the development is determined, the review process must include analysis of:

● The zoning of the area ● The overall layout and design by a group of city planners ● The profile of the community surrounding the area (social and economic characteristics) ● The community’s opinions on the development ● The guidelines and laws in place in that area (noise specifications, building regulations,

etc.) ● The environmental factors of the area

○ How the development effect these factors and is affected by the climate, and

potential emergencies or disasters ● The effect of the development on the capacity of public transportation

A successful waterfront designed for a community should not be a series of detached attractions and spaces, but a concise and well-connected space with different areas that relate to each other. Once the thorough analysis by specialized professionals knowledgeable in each of the subjects is completed, then a second review must be done in order to finalize the overall goal of the establishment in accordance with the findings. It should be a cyclical review rather than a direct line where the more information is found, the more areas there are to explore and the more professionals to consult. It is key and essential for this process to be meticulously done and reviewed by different entities and stakeholders. A diverse review panel is also essential for the conclusions to be well-rounded and well-founded. The more in depth this process is, the more successful the waterfront development will be.

### 5.3 Maintaining Communication Across Waterfront Entities

In each of the cities we researched, the ownership of the waterfront varied from public land to privately leased or owned land. However, each city was able to create an open environment with a seamless interaction between their public and private entities. The instrumental factor for this was maintaining communication across all waterfront entities. The communication between the public government and the private developers must be clear and the goal for the waterfront must be directly communicated to developers.

5.3.1 The Importance of Guidelines

Communicating these goals from the city to the developers is done through existing regulations and zoning by-laws. These guidelines exist to force developers to create an open space along the waterfront. This is especially important in locations where the government leases land out to private developers, but does not include any clauses in the lease regarding maintaining an open and public waterfront. This has led many profit driven developers to invest in upper class residencies with private yards, as well as high class hotels with private patios along the waterfront, destroying the accessibility of the space. These guidelines must be in place to guarantee that the space along the waterfront will remain public. They must be easy-to-access, legible, and must clearly portray the city’s goals using specific and detailed terminology in order to properly display what the waterfront should look like in the future. Specificity is key to limit variation in the interpretation of the guidelines and ensures that there are nor inconsistencies between developments, especially during changes in leadership. Some examples include:

● Requiring open spaces directly along the waterfront to be available for public use. ● Specific designs, dimensions, and locations for outdoor dining. ● Requiring roads, promenades, and other paths to be seamlessly integrated with the

rest of the city. ● Specific requirements for the width and design of footpaths. ● Requiring shading for a percentage of public seating along the waterfront.

These guidelines should be specific and reflect the city’s intentions of maintaining an open waterfront. The more specific the regulations, the easier it is to ensure that the entire waterfront district will be a cohesive and inviting space.

5.3.2 Upholding the Guidelines

Laws and regulations must be upheld to ensure that they are effective. To ensure that developers align with the goal of the city, the multi-step review process mentioned above is key. This will act as a strict process for the plans to ensure that they follow all of the regulations in place, fit the atmosphere of the waterfront, and will incorporate with the rest of the existing waterfront elements. If a plan were to fail this review process, it would be given back to the


<!-- Page 56 -->


46

developers along with feedback. When revised the plans can be reevaluated by the review board. Maintaining this rigorous communication between the public and private entities is also essential to creating a cohesive, open, and inviting space along the entire waterfront.

Effective processes include a single group to review designs as multiple review boards across a single waterfront allow for conflicting interest and result in a less cohesive waterfront. In cities with multiple groups controlling the waterfront, inconsistencies about the expectations of each of them grow quickly. There are a host of opportunities for miscommunication between the entities which can lead to issues integrating different waterfront districts together, poor maintenance on the waterfront, and an especially slow development process. A single controlling entity allows the waterfront to share the same goal across its entire length, and limits the opportunities for miscommunication between different groups. Community feedback is also vital in this stage as the guidelines may not always reflect what the intended audience for the waterfront is interested in. Looping the neighbors and the community into the development process allows them to weigh in on future plans and help shape the space into an environment that they will enjoy.
